content: 1. The quantities of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs received during a reporting period include both procured and donated supplies. It is essential to assess whether the received quantities align with the forecasted supply needs. If the received quantities exceed the planned amounts, there is a risk of drug expiration and wastage. Conversely, if the received quantities are less than planned, stock-outs may occur, potentially limiting program scale-up. 2. The consumption of ARV drugs during a reporting period is measured to evaluate the correlation between the quantities received and consumed. If the quantities on hand exceed program usage, there is a risk of overstock and potential losses due to expiration. On the other hand, if consumption exceeds available stock and buffer stock is depleted, stock-outs will occur. 3. Procurement efficiency is assessed by comparing the median price paid by a country for the preferred first-line ARV regimen to the median price of the same regimen in the region. A ratio below 1, which decreases over time, indicates efficient procurement. A ratio above 1 suggests the country is paying more than others in the region, warranting further investigation. 4. Supplier performance is evaluated by the percentage of orders delivered on time and in full (OTIF) during a reporting period. This metric assesses the supplier's ability to meet delivery schedules and specified quantities as per procurement contracts. The data can be further disaggregated by supplier for detailed analysis. 5. Port clearance performance is measured by the percentage of orders cleared within the defined deadline. Timely clearance of goods from the port is critical, as delays can lead to drug deterioration and contribute to stock-outs. 6. The registration of ARV drugs is assessed by the percentage of recommended ARV formulations registered in the country. This includes preferred formulations for adults and optimal pediatric formulations. Registration is vital to improving access to and affordability of these drugs. 7. The distribution system's performance is evaluated by the percentage of ART sites that received all orders OTIF from central or regional stores during a reporting period. This metric reflects the effectiveness of the national distribution system in supplying ARV medicines to health facilities. 8. Inventory control is assessed by the percentage of ART sites that submitted complete inventory control reports on time during the reporting period. Timely reporting is crucial for the effective functioning of procurement and supply management systems, as well as for monitoring and evaluation (M&E). 9. Losses in the procurement and supply management system are measured by the percentage of procured ARV quantities lost due to expiration, damage, diversion, or theft. If losses exceed 1%, further analysis of the causes and corrective actions is required. 10. The minimum stock level is assessed by the percentage of ART sites that placed orders when their stock was below the minimum level. This metric evaluates the effectiveness of the logistics management information system. Placing orders below the minimum stock level increases the risk of stock-outs. 11. Strategic information systems are reviewed to identify available and missing data, which informs planning and enables improvements in the system. This review reflects the commitment of national authorities to base decisions on accurate information. 12. The percentage of indicator data published annually is a measure of the willingness of national authorities to share information with stakeholders. This transparency is critical for accountability and collaboration. 13. The completion of the National Commitments and Policies Instrument (NCPI) questionnaire for HIV/AIDS assesses whether the country has a multisectoral strategic plan that covers all sectors and target populations, involves civil society, is endorsed by external development partners, aligns with the national strategy, and integrates into other development plans. 14. The completion of WHO HIV health sector response policy questions focuses on health sector-specific issues, such as ART, PMTCT, key populations, and M&E. This tool is useful for decision-making within the Ministry of Health. 15. Domestic financing for the HIV response is measured by the percentage of HIV funding sourced domestically. This metric reflects the country's ownership and willingness to finance its HIV response. Tracking this over time provides insights into trends in domestic ownership. 16. The proportion of HIV spending in the national health budget indicates the prioritization of HIV health activities. This metric explores options to increase contributions from public and international health financing to HIV programs. 17. Progress in domestic financing is tracked using the Relative Variation Index, which measures trends in self-sustained responses to HIV, with a focus on ART and prevention among key populations. A result greater than 1 signifies progress in domestic financing. 18. The contribution of domestic private sources to HIV financing is measured by the percentage of domestic private expenditure. This metric highlights the role of private sources in diversifying and increasing funding for HIV programs. 19. The unit cost of HIV interventions is assessed by per capita expenditure on specific HIV health programs. Over time, this metric monitors changes in average expenditure per person reached or service delivered. It can be benchmarked against countries with similar income levels or epidemic burdens.
